Why Should Anyone Need a License for Anything? | Kevin Currie-Knight

I think there are a lot of practical issues this article doesn't touch on. Licensing is, by its very nature, a monopolistic venture. Having 1000 different licensing bodies is as good as having 0. The most successful licensor would invariably become the standard. The people in charge of the licensing agency have certainly been fully competitive and up the up and up, until the point they 'win'. Now they know they're effectively shielded from competitors by a massive and completely organic barrier - mindshare of the public. And now introduce a profit incentive. Suddenly a license costs you 10% of your revenue.

This is a major issue in areas where barriers to entry organically arise. How much do you pay for fire service? Pretty much nothing. How much would you pay if it was privatized? In theory, you'd pay about the same. In reality the company that became the most 'reputable' fire fighting agency would have an organic monopoly as most are not going to skimp when it comes to the safety of their property - and you'd likely end up paying far more as this monopoly was flexed. Any competitor would have to overcome the organic monopoly of public mindshare and that's an enormous barrier. Not to mention the established monopolist would also benefit from a sort of economy of scale. They'd have more trucks, more stations, and generally more capacity to provide a greater service everywhere.

Another practical issue. What happens when somebody says they're licensed by you, and they're not? They're ruining the value of your 'product' and unfairly enriching themselves. Are we supposed to call on government to enforce the terms and qualifications for licensors? In which case the licensor is quickly acting as little more than a middle man or proxy for government, except one tha'ts taking a cut of the profits - somewhat similar to Obamacare and healthcare insurers. Or do we expect customers to come exclusively to our site to find 'officially' licensed practitioners in which case we further strengthen the monopoly and organic barriers to entry?

These issues may be surmountable, but I don't see any immediately clear resolution. In any case I think discussing the practical negatives is far more reasonable than simply pretending something is a dream solution when it most certainly is not.
